prompt: Evaluate the extent to which the government under the Articles of Confederation was effective in addressing the challenges facing the United States in the period 1781-1789.

documents.title: Articles of Confederation, Article III
documents.source: Articles of Confederation, Article III, adopted by Congress November 15, 1777. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The frame of government itself, written as the states broke from Britain and wary of any distant authority.
documents.text: “The said States hereby severally enter into a firm league of friendship with each other, for their common defence, the security of their Liberties, and their mutual and general welfare, binding themselves to assist each other, against all force offered to, or attacks made upon them, or any of them, on account of religion, sovereignty, trade, or any other pretence whatever.”

documents.title: Articles of Confederation, Article VIII
documents.source: Articles of Confederation, Article VIII, adopted by Congress November 15, 1777 (abridged). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The revenue article of the same frame of government, showing how Congress was meant to pay for itself.
documents.text: “All charges of war, and all other expenses that shall be incurred for the common defense or general welfare, and allowed by the United States in Congress assembled, shall be defrayed out of a common treasury, which shall be supplied by the several States in proportion to the value of all land within each State. . . . The taxes for paying that proportion shall be laid and levied by the authority and direction of the legislatures of the several States within the time agreed upon by the United States in Congress assembled.”

documents.title: Northwest Ordinance, Article VI
documents.source: Northwest Ordinance, Article VI, July 13, 1787. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A law passed by the Confederation Congress itself, two months before the Constitution was signed.
documents.text: “There shall be neither slavery nor involuntary servitude in the said territory, otherwise than in the punishment of crimes, whereof the party shall have been duly convicted: Provided, always, That any person escaping into the same, from whom labor or service is lawfully claimed in any one of the original States, such fugitive may be lawfully reclaimed, and conveyed to the person claiming his or her labor or service as aforesaid.”

documents.title: Shays's forces fleeing troops at Springfield
documents.source: C. Kendrick, Shays's forces fleeing troops at Springfield, c. 1902. Public domain (pre-1930 publication).
documents.sourcing: An engraving made about a century after the event, picturing how the rebellion ended at Springfield in 1787.
documents.text: The engraving shows armed farmers fleeing through a village street in Springfield, Massachusetts, as uniformed troops with a cannon advance behind them. The farmers, many carrying muskets, run past bare winter trees and a white house.

documents.title: George Washington on the tumults in Massachusetts
documents.source: George Washington to Henry Lee, Jr., Mount Vernon, October 31, 1786. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A private letter from the most respected American, written at the height of Shays's Rebellion to a member of Congress.
documents.text: “You talk, my good Sir, of employing influence to appease the present tumults in Massachusetts. I know not where that influence is to be found, or, if attainable, that it would be a proper remedy for the disorders. Influence is no government. Let us have one by which our lives, liberties, and properties will be secured, or let us know the worst at once.”

documents.title: Report of the Annapolis Convention
documents.source: Report of the Commissioners to Remedy Defects of the Federal Government, Annapolis, September 14, 1786 (abridged). Public domain.
documents.sourcing: The report of commissioners from five states who met to discuss trade and found they could not act.
documents.text: “Your Commissioners did not conceive it advisable to proceed on the business of their mission, under the Circumstance of so partial and defective a representation. . . . Your Commissioners, with the most respectful deference, beg leave to suggest their unanimous conviction, that it may essentially tend to advance the interests of the union, if the States . . . would themselves concur, and use their endeavours to procure the concurrence of the other States, in the appointment of Commissioners, to meet at Philadelphia on the second Monday in May next, to take into consideration the situation of the United States, to devise such further provisions as shall appear to them necessary to render the constitution of the Federal Government adequate to the exigencies of the Union.”

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which the government under the Articles was effective in addressing the challenges of 1781-1789, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the war for independence and its debts, the fear of distant authority after British rule, or the writing of new state constitutions.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing the content of at least three documents relevant to the argument about how effective the Articles government was.
rubric.notEarned: Quoting documents without describing what they show does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support the argument, including documents showing both effectiveness and failure.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or using six without tying them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific relevant example not in the documents, such as the failure of Robert Morris's 5 percent impost, Britain keeping its western forts, Spain closing the Mississippi to American trade, or the Land Ordinance of 1785.
rubric.notEarned: A vague reference to outside knowledge with no specific example does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining how the audience, purpose, historical situation, or point of view of at least two documents shapes the argument, such as Washington's private alarm, the Annapolis report's call for a new convention, or the Kendrick engraving as a later picture of the rebellion.
rubric.notEarned: Naming a document's author without explaining how it shapes the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for a complex argument, such as qualifying the thesis by challenge, showing where the Articles government succeeded with western lands and where it failed with money, order, and trade.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: The government under the Articles was effective at only one of its great challenges: it organized the western lands, but it failed at money, order, and trade, so its effectiveness was narrow and its failures forced its replacement.
Context: The United States came out of the war for independence in debt and wary of distant authority. The Articles were written to keep power close to home, with a league of sovereign states and no power to tax.
Evidence of failure: Document 2 shows the revenue system depended on the states, and the states paid late or not at all. Document 5 shows Washington calling influence no government during Shays's Rebellion. Document 4 shows the rebellion put down by force outside Congress's power. Document 6 shows reformers at Annapolis unable to act on trade and calling for a new convention.
Evidence of effectiveness: Document 7 shows the states ceding their western claims to create a national domain. Document 3 shows the Northwest Ordinance banning slavery north of the Ohio and setting a path to statehood. Document 1 shows the league the states agreed to, which held them together through the war.
Beyond the documents: Robert Morris's 5 percent impost failed because amendments needed all thirteen states, and Britain kept its western forts while Spain closed the Mississippi to American trade.
Complexity: The Articles succeeded exactly where the states agreed to give up something, the western lands, and failed everywhere the government needed to act on its own, with money, troops, and trade.
